# What the Architect Owns {#sec-what-architect-owns}

::: {.epigraph}
> "The second irony is that the designer who tries to eliminate the operator still leaves the operator to do the tasks which the designer cannot think how to automate."
>
> — Lisanne Bainbridge, *Ironies of Automation* [@Bainbridge1983Ironies, p. 775]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *If AI can perform substantial design work, what do architects still contribute and remain responsible for?*

**Core thesis:** *Architectural ownership resides in framing problems, setting abstractions, judging cross-layer trade-offs, and governing commitment to silicon.*
:::

Architects turn product needs into system designs. They choose the problem, develop abstractions and alternatives, connect software behavior to physical consequences, and reconcile the trade-offs across components. An AI-native design system may contribute to all of that work, including proposing better formulations and organizations. The architect's responsibility is to develop and defend a coherent system recommendation, even if automation can generate the register-transfer level (RTL), search the configurations, and complete the implementation checks.

That recommendation and the decision to act on it remain distinct (@fig-ch11-cover-map). A *technical recommendation* explains whether a candidate serves the product's requirements, what alternatives were considered, and what remains uncertain. *Commitment authority* belongs to a named person authorized to freeze an interface, accept residual risk, or tape out the design. A leading-edge mask set alone is estimated in the tens of millions of dollars [@Patel2022MaskSetCosts], so fabrication commits substantial capital before any wafer is measured. Neither a favorable tool report nor a demonstrated workflow advantage (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect) makes that decision automatically.

![**Architectural ownership separates candidate evaluation from commitment authority.** An AI-native design system and domain specialists explore candidate spaces and verify implementations, but architects own problem formulation, abstraction boundaries, and cross-layer trade-offs. The resulting system recommendation provides qualified evidence to an authorized organizational decision maker rather than committing resources automatically.](images/ch11-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch11-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which substantial AI-native design work and architectural ownership remain distinct from a named commitment authority inside an accountable organization."}

The recommendation itself rests on checks that other people run. Domain specialists establish what their checks support, while the architect connects those findings across the system and investigates interactions that no single check covers. Because the resulting recommendation remains bounded by the implementation and conditions those checks cover, integration, deployment, and later changes to the workload or operating conditions can invalidate that basis, so architectural ownership includes deciding when to reopen the recommendation. Delegation must therefore preserve the technical understanding and access needed to revise both the design and its recommendation.

## Delegating Without Losing Technical Contact {#sec-delegating-without-losing-contact}

Delegation does not remove responsibility for deciding what to build, because specifying the right target remains as central a difficulty in hardware as in software engineering [@Brooks1986NoSilverBullet]. While an automated system may help formulate the problem, propose alternatives, and assemble evidence for a recommendation, the people responsible for the product still decide whether that recommendation addresses the right needs and warrants commitment. This division of authority rests on accountability for the product rather than on any assumption that human proposals are better than automated ones.

Exercising that accountability requires technical judgment that engineers in conventional workflows build by writing RTL, inspecting waveforms, and iterating with electronic design automation (EDA) tools. That hands-on contact shows them directly how microarchitectural choices turn into routing congestion and timing slack. When a team delegates candidate drafting, macro floorplanning, and regression sweeps to automated loops, the contact moves away from the engineer. The architect need not repeat every automated step by hand, but must still be able to inspect the specific traces, floorplans, and assumptions that could overturn the recommendation.

Four questions help determine how much work can be delegated and what must be checked before acting on its results:

1. **Observability**: Can the architect inspect the candidate, its evaluation conditions, and the traces supporting the recommendation?
2. **Reversibility**: Which changes can be rolled back cleanly, and which would require costly rework once accepted?
3. **Independent checks**: What checks could expose errors in the proposal or its evaluation, and which assumptions do those checks share with the automated loop?
4. **Bounded consequences**: Which cross-layer effects have been evaluated, and which remain outside the study's scope?

The answers depend on the scope of the delegated work (@sec-three-operational-layers). An engineer can inspect a generated arithmetic block and restore its previous revision. A broad hardware–software redesign instead requires access to interface contracts, execution traces, counterexamples, and physical reports; line-by-line inspection alone cannot establish that its components work together. In either case, the team must preserve a known integration version and control which changes may enter the product design.

That check on incoming changes becomes especially important as decisions approach interface freeze, where reversibility narrows. A bounded array-mapping sweep or a focused tool run leaves interfaces open. Freezing an instruction set architecture (ISA) contract or fixing the physical-layer lane count on a 2.5D Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) link[^fn-ucie-phy-c11] hardens assumptions across compiler runtimes, memory hierarchies, RTL, floorplans, and product thermals at once. Before the responsible lead authorizes such a freeze, the architect must reconcile evidence across every one of those coupled layers.

[^fn-ucie-phy-c11]: **Die-to-die physical layers and interconnect budgeting**: In multi-die systems, Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) defines physical layer (PHY) lane widths, channel reach, and bump pitches ($100\text{--}130\ \mu\text{m}$ for standard packages and $25\text{--}55\ \mu\text{m}$ for advanced 2.5D packaging such as silicon interposers or bridges) [@DasSharma2024UCIe20Introduction]. Freezing PHY lane counts constrains die-edge allocation, substrate routing layers, and escape routing. Bandwidth can still change through supported link rates within the qualified operating envelope; adding lanes would reopen those allocations, which is our reasoning rather than a statement of the specification.

Reconciling those layers requires direct technical contact across tool boundaries. Without that contact, an engineer has no basis for calibrating trust in automation, and human-factors research names the two resulting failures *misuse* (inappropriate reliance on automation) and *disuse* (neglecting automation capabilities entirely) [@ParasuramanRiley1997HumansAutomation]. Good abstractions do not remove the need. Logic synthesis and hardware construction languages provide powerful ways to express and implement designs [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization; @Izraelevitz2017Chisel], yet engineers working through any abstraction still need to challenge the problem formulation, inspect decisive failure traces, and recognize physical effects the model omits. As automated loops absorb routine microarchitectural sweeps and propose broader redesigns, that diagnostic access is how architects identify missing constraints, develop cross-layer alternatives, and judge whether the combined evidence supports a system recommendation.

The same delegation creates an apprenticeship risk. Junior engineers who encounter designs only through prompts and scorecards may never build the diagnostic experience needed to challenge a result or recommend a consequential change [@Bainbridge1983Ironies]. Training curricula must therefore give them deliberate opportunities to investigate failures (@sec-curriculum-certification).

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Judgment precedes and governs automation"}
**The principle:** Automation may formulate problems, explore alternatives, implement designs, and analyze systems. Architects must retain the technical understanding needed to challenge and revise the problem, the abstraction, and the system boundaries as results emerge.

**The application:** A review supporting a commitment should explain how the component results support one feasible system recommendation and what evidence could overturn it. It should identify the architect responsible for that recommendation and the commitment authority responsible for the organizational decision.
:::

## Framing Cross-Layer Problems {#sec-framing-architecture-problem}

If an architect gives an automated optimizer a narrow, single-layer objective such as maximizing neural processing unit (NPU) matrix-array utilization, the search can return a configuration that wins on that metric and fails as a system. Its bursty direct memory access (DMA) traffic can saturate the LPDDR5 memory bus, starve the host CPU, and push package power past 3\ W. The architect's judgment therefore enters first in framing the problem that an automated design loop will explore. The architect defines the system boundary, identifies the governing cross-layer interactions, decides which physical consequences the evaluation must measure, and revisits those choices when generated candidates and tool runs reveal missing constraints or better organizations. The choice of mechanisms and interfaces frames the design space itself, as the case for a reduced instruction set showed [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC], so the architect's role extends beyond bounding the physical hardware. The architect also designs the decision workflow: which methods propose candidate modifications, which modeling tools estimate their properties, which validation checks screen candidates, and how the team investigates cross-layer disagreements.

To see how problem framing shapes that workflow, recall how @sec-intent-vs-spec decomposed the Lighthouse extended-reality (XR) specification request, "Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for a real-time mobile XR workload," across eight requirement domains. Consider a candidate organization that combines a host CPU with an NPU across a UCIe packaging link. That template is one possible organization rather than a choice settled by the request, and how deeply the team must evaluate it depends on the commitment at stake.

A freeze decision asks far more of the requirement decomposition than a local exploration does. Studying array utilization requires only cycle-level modeling and mapping search, whereas freezing that array alongside its software interface and packaging link demands evidence that the selected parts work together as a subsystem. Before recommending a freeze, the architect must trace how compiler lowering through Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) shapes the memory traffic. The architect must then check whether the resulting execution meets timing and stays within the total 3\ W subsystem thermal design power (TDP) limit. While IP review and non-recurring engineering (NRE) capital review add organizational conditions for proceeding, the specific architecture question determines which technical models and checks must run to support the recommendation.

Across decisions of this kind, eight recurring judgments help turn isolated tool results into one coherent recommendation (@tbl-architect-technical-judgments). Each row pairs a question the architect must answer with the coupling it exposes in the host CPU and NPU candidate, so that missing constraints, cross-layer trade-offs, and residual risk surface before anyone decides to commit.

| **Judgment** | **Architectural question** | **Lighthouse consequence** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Problem choice and reframing** | Is the stated problem still the one the product needs solved? | Deciding whether the goal is maximizing raw NPU general matrix multiply (GEMM) utilization or meeting the mobile XR workload's frame deadlines within a 3\ W TDP envelope. |
| **Abstraction** | Which details can be simplified for this decision? | A cycle-level NPU model can compare matrix mappings locally, but a freeze decision must also account for Triton/LLVM/MLIR compiler lowering, static random-access memory (SRAM) / LPDDR5 memory traffic, UCIe interconnect energy, physical timing, and the 3\ W subsystem boundary. |
| **System boundary** | Where do workload, software, hardware, package, physical design, and product effects meet? | Deciding whether NPU array sizing can be analyzed in isolation, or must encompass host 64-bit RISC-V application core with vector extensions (RV64GCV) task dispatch, UCIe chiplet routing, dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) bandwidth contention, and packaging thermal limits. |
| **Architecture synthesis** | Do chosen mechanisms, interfaces, software paths, and implementation choices form one feasible system? | Confirming that the NPU matrix engine, RV64GCV CPU contract, compiler lowering pipeline, LPDDR5 memory subsystem, and firmware fallback paths form a coherent, manufacturable subsystem. |
| **Missing constraints** | What has the formulation, representation, or tool path left out? | Uncovering omitted physical and legal factors: transient voltage droop in the power delivery network (PDN), 3\ W thermal dissipation limits, UCIe signal integrity, IP indemnification, and post-silicon fallback controls (chicken-bits). |
| **Cross-layer trade-off** | Which feasible point best serves the product when objectives conflict? | Resolving the tension between host RV64GCV vector tail latency, NPU matrix throughput, LPDDR5 memory power, UCIe die-to-die routing congestion, and manual review burden. |
| **Mechanism and consequence** | Does the proposed explanation fit the observations, and what happens if it is wrong? | Evaluating whether an apparent speedup is driven by architectural dataflow or an unmodeled memory wait state, where an erroneous tapeout freeze risks new masks and a few more months of fabrication [@Patel2022MaskSetCosts]. |
| **Commitment under uncertainty** | Are remaining risks understood, containable, and worth accepting? | Recommending against physical tapeout when static timing closure, formal property bounds, IP indemnification, and power delivery margins remain uncharacterized. |
: **Architecture judgment gives technical work its system meaning.** Architects choose the question, abstraction, boundary, and consequence before the commitment authority decides whether the design advances. {#tbl-architect-technical-judgments tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

In practice, these eight judgments expose where a feasibility claim rests on physical coupling that individual models left out. In our hypothetical CPU-NPU-UCIe candidate, the team does not yet know whether NPU DMA burst sizing, LPDDR5 bus contention, host CPU interrupt latency, and package thermal gradients allow the XR workload to meet its frame deadlines inside a 3\ W thermal envelope. Because simplified abstractions routinely hide bottlenecks that cross block boundaries, identifying those interactions early tells the architect which models are safe to trust and which additional implementation checks the recommendation needs.

## Selecting System Abstractions and Bounds {#sec-selecting-abstractions-constraints}

Once the system boundaries are set, the architect chooses the representations and analytical models that govern exploration, because every architectural model is defined as much by what it omits as by what it represents. While a memory trace in Ramulator [@KimEtAl2015Ramulator] can expose channel contention and an NPU dataflow model in SCALE-Sim [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3] shows how a mapping occupies the array, neither view alone establishes physical timing or thermal feasibility. Moving to RTL simulation, physical implementation tools, and a package thermal model adds those physical observations, but it also creates a reconciliation problem because the workload, interfaces, and operating conditions must agree across every view. When the architect selects an abstraction, the task therefore includes naming the omitted details that could flip the decision and scheduling a check that can observe them.

Choosing an abstraction also fixes what architectural state each predictor, generator, optimizer, or tool is allowed to modify and which measurements constrain those edits. Consider a learned macro placer such as AlphaChip [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. If a team configured a hypothetical NPU placement objective that omitted power delivery network (PDN) and package-thermal effects, the optimizer could cluster high-activity vector units where transient supply droop threatens timing, or return a layout that exceeds the combined package's thermal limit. Because the objective function never measured those physical consequences, neither effect would lower its placement score, so both require separate signoff checks. That need does not depend on the separate dispute over whether AlphaChip beats tuned conventional placers on a matched baseline [@ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment; @GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed]. A generator given direct control over standard-cell placement likewise requires checks for foundry design rules, well spacing, and available routing tracks, which is why across both macro and standard-cell flows the architect defines block boundaries, curates macro sets, sets timing and power constraints across host CPU and NPU cores, chooses comparison baselines, and arranges physical signoff.

Those boundaries and permitted edits can also fail in the opposite direction, limiting a search even when the relevant constraint is known. When an optimizer is confined to a fixed template and none of its permitted parameter choices relieves a saturated memory interface, the search stalls at that template's boundary. Authorizing a different organization expands the design possibilities, but also requires representations and checks that cover its new interfaces and physical effects. The architect must establish that scope before relying on the redesigned system.

Beyond choosing models for individual tools, architects govern how components interact by defining interface contracts, assigning revision authority, selecting independent signoff checks, and auditing shared assumptions across verification steps. Many consequential constraints originate as unwritten engineering experience [@Polanyi1966TacitDimension, p. 4]: compiler leads may know that a proposed matrix opcode lacks an efficient lowering path, while physical-design leads recognize power-grid heuristics that break down on dense CPU-NPU floorplans. Language models can help locate, compare, and organize these scattered expert judgments for formal review. Any constraint that shapes the design, however, still requires verification checks matched to its risk and scope, whether automated checkers, conventional EDA tools, domain specialists, or peer reviewers run them.

Once the team accepts such a constraint, the commitment record should state its source, its scope, the interfaces it affects, its known conflicts, and the conditions that would reopen it. Suppose a physical designer's rule bars placing two high-current macros on the same power stripe for a given metal stack and operating threshold. The architect decides how to enforce that rule in the floorplanner and evaluates the resulting routing overhead. If the project later moves to a new power-grid template or a 3D stacked die, the physical assumptions behind that rule no longer hold, which triggers a fresh review rather than leaving an obsolete restriction in force. Recording the constraint together with its operating assumptions keeps an optimizer from quietly violating an unwritten physical limit, yet lets the team retire that limit when the technology changes instead of rejecting valid designs. Even well-chosen models and constraints, however, evaluate only one view of the hardware at a time; the architect still has to integrate their separate outputs into a single working system.

## Governing System Integration {#sec-orchestrating-system-integration}

A design candidate becomes a viable architecture, rather than an assortment of isolated optimizations, only when its mechanisms and interfaces hold together under the physical and logical conditions of the full stack. Automated methods can reason across layers when those interactions are represented and checked, but any result from a tool or domain specialist covers only the interactions its model includes. An NPU array optimization that omits host CPU cache coherence, memory channel contention, or UCIe chiplet thermal dissipation cannot establish feasibility across those boundaries. The architect has to set and challenge the scope of those studies, expose missing interactions, and compose specialized results into a unified system recommendation.

Consider a hypothetical revision of the Lighthouse XR system-on-chip (SoC). Trace analyses in gem5 and SCALE-Sim support the frame deadlines, MLIR compiler searches yield legal NPU tiling, Verilator RTL simulations pass, Ramulator memory models satisfy local bandwidth checks, OpenSTA reports that timing constraints are met, and power-aware checks using Unified Power Format (UPF) [@IEEE2024UPF] verify the declared power-gating behavior. Each check passes in isolation, yet combining the results exposes two cross-layer faults. The burst memory traffic introduced by the new NPU tiling pushes estimated subsystem power across SRAM arrays, UCIe links, and LPDDR5 channels past the 3\ W thermal envelope, and a critical tail-latency path has no software fallback.

To resolve those faults, the architect proposes coordinated adjustments across the stack: assigning tail-latency handling to the host CPU core, narrowing NPU DMA bursts, rebalancing memory buffers, and specifying firmware fallback paths. Each adjustment creates a new cross-layer obligation of its own. Narrower bursts relieve memory contention at the expense of accelerator throughput and must be re-evaluated against the frame deadline; moving work to the host CPU requires checking its scheduling and power draw under concurrent load; and rebalancing buffers requires checking capacity and backpressure under the revised traffic pattern. The firmware fallback path must likewise preserve functional correctness, with its latency and power costs measured under the conditions in which it runs. A different kind of fallback, programmable control-register overrides (often called *chicken-bits*), offers a post-silicon way to disable a faulty speculative path, but only if verification proves that flipping the override actually contains the fault. Working through these coupled checks turns a collection of local passes into a candidate system whose end-to-end interactions can be tested.

The resulting recommendation explains why the revised subsystem should meet its requirements and identifies any checks that still disagree. Those remaining disagreements deserve close attention before a preferred candidate advances, because they often expose a broken interface assumption that no single-domain optimization examined.

## Resolving Cross-Layer Discrepancies {#sec-resolving-discrepancies}

When models across different domains disagree, the conflict may expose incompatible assumptions, competing approximations, or a candidate that genuinely improves one metric while failing another requirement. If a cycle-level simulator reports performance gains for a new NPU array mapping while physical signoff tools report power-grid voltage droop under concurrent host CPU vector loads, both tools may be right, and the faster mapping is still infeasible under realistic system load. The architect cannot average those metrics, nor, under schedule pressure, pick the more convenient report to dismiss a blocking failure. Architectural judgment begins instead by asking what each result actually establishes. Before the design can advance, the team must explain the physical mechanism behind the conflict, reexamine the model abstractions, run a check that separates the competing explanations, or hold the candidate until the blocking discrepancy is resolved.

Three steps help separate a candidate defect from a disagreement about what the tools checked:

1. **Contract and condition alignment**: The architect and domain specialists identify the requirement each check addresses and compare implementation versions, workloads, operating conditions, and assumptions. A valid failure of any applicable blocking requirement rules out the candidate under those conditions, even when checks of other requirements pass, because a pass on one requirement cannot offset a failure on another.
2. **Abstraction correction**: When checks encode inconsistent assumptions or interfaces, the team determines which representation departs from the intended product contract, corrects the erroneous abstraction, model, or interface definition, and reruns the affected tool paths. If the contract itself is ambiguous, the architect resolves its meaning against the product requirements before rerunning the checks rather than weakening a valid requirement to obtain a pass.
3. **Investigation of unresolved discrepancies**: When formal proofs and cycle-accurate models still disagree about an interface invariant, the team selects an observation that can distinguish the competing explanations. If the discrepancy cannot be resolved within verification budgets, the candidate remains blocked from advancing past the affected check, and the architect and affected specialists record what remains unexplained before signoff.

Suppose a coherence verifier using SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) and bounded model checking (BMC) returns a counterexample within $k = 50$ cycles against a blocking property between host CPU caches and NPU DMA stores.[^fn-bmc-c11] A high-level software model, meanwhile, treats the same execution as legal under high-contention LPDDR5 traffic. Neither the architect nor an automated loop may weaken the property, discard the failing workload, or relabel the counterexample as passing. To resolve the conflict between the formal check and the software model, we ask whether both tools encode the same product contract and permit the memory events in the counterexample. Tracing how the software model represents those exact memory events locates where the two views diverge. If the counterexample reflects behavior the candidate hardware can produce and violates a valid blocking requirement, the candidate fails; otherwise, the team corrects the erroneous representation or resolves the contract ambiguity and reruns both paths.

That resolution assumes the property itself is correct, which no longer holds automatically when generative models propose both the candidate RTL and the formal assertions. Verification engineers must then check the blocking assertions against the product contract independently of the generated RTL. Mutation testing (@sec-semantic-rtl-defects) can measure the harness's sensitivity to injected faults [@DeMilloLiptonSayward1978Hints], but cannot rule out specification omissions shared by the candidate and its checkers.

[^fn-bmc-c11]: **Bounded model checking and SystemVerilog Assertions**: SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) express formal properties to check. Bounded model checking (BMC) searches for a property violation within a specified number of unrolled execution cycles under encoded assumptions; a completed passing check establishes the absence of a counterexample within that finite bound, not an inductive proof at arbitrary depth [@BiereEtAl1999BMC; @SymbiYosys].

A different discrepancy arises when feasible candidates pass their blocking checks but return overlapping estimates for tail latency and subsystem power. Here the architect asks whether workload sampling, model error, or untested operating corners could flip which design wins. The right response is to run the least costly check with enough fidelity to separate the candidates on the specific uncertainty that could change the recommendation: matched cycle-level trace runs in gem5 for workload-dependent timing, physical thermal simulations for heat buildup, OpenSTA static timing runs for path slack, or post-layout power-grid analyses for voltage droop. If the available checks cannot resolve the overlap within budget, the architect keeps the recommendation narrow and favors choices that remain reversible. Once these discrepancies and uncertainties are resolved or explicitly bounded, the architect has a qualified hardware recommendation, which raises the separate governance question of what that evidence actually authorizes.

## Separating Evidence from Commitments {#sec-linking-results-claims-commitments}

The architect connects hardware evidence to project governance through the recommendation, presenting the preferred candidate alongside evaluated alternatives, explaining the cross-layer trade-offs, documenting boundary conditions and signoff checks, and stating the remaining uncertainties. While the architect owns that cross-layer synthesis, domain specialists remain responsible for the validity and scope of their underlying signoffs across timing closure, power integrity, physical implementation, and reliability.

When that combined hardware record reaches a review, two of the meanings of progress in @sec-efficiency-claims-need-rejectable-loops still require independent judgments. Whether the complete approach adds methodological value is a program claim that carries an evidence status such as *supported* or *unresolved* (@sec-negative-claims-scope-limits), whereas the commitment decision belongs to the people authorized to commit the project after they weigh the recommendation, trade-offs, result limits, and residual risk.

Keeping these judgments separate protects each decision from the other, in both directions. Even when a workflow claim is *supported*, a faster search or a better Pareto frontier does not compel a silicon commitment if physical thermals, organizational capacity, or business risks remain unacceptable. Conversely, an *unresolved* workflow comparison does not prevent an organization from committing to a sound hardware architecture backed by thorough physical signoff. Because an evidence status never records a product decision, every recommendation must identify who is authorized to approve the next transition and present the specific hardware evidence that transition requires.

## Governing Tapeout Commitments {#sec-governing-tapeout-commitments}

What a commitment requires depends on how much of the design the next transition locks in. Moving from high-level exploration toward physical silicon progressively freezes interfaces, bus contracts, and floorplans. Early in the design cycle, changing ISA extensions or buffer layouts means editing software models or RTL. After freeze, a change to the reticles pays for at least some new masks, generally on the critical layers, and takes a few months [@Patel2022MaskSetCosts]. The supporting evidence must therefore address the consequences that will become hardest to reverse.

::: {.callout-war-story title="An architecture can outlast its original product plan"}
**The claim.** Larrabee described a many-core x86 architecture for visual computing, with wide vector units, coherent caches, and a software rendering pipeline that replaced fixed-function steps such as rasterization [@SeilerEtAl2008Larrabee]. In September 2009, Intel demonstrated Larrabee silicon and described plans for discrete graphics products [@Intel2009LarrabeeDemonstration].

**The gap.** In May 2010, Intel announced Many Integrated Core product plans targeting high-performance computing and identified Larrabee as one of the projects from which the architecture was derived [@Intel2010MICPlans]. A working silicon demonstration therefore did not settle which product the architecture would serve. The public record does not disclose the internal evidence or capital-allocation rationale behind that change.

**The lesson.** Reusing an architecture and committing to a particular product are different decisions. A recommendation must identify the target workload, product requirements, and remaining expenditure for the proposed transition.
:::

Because each transition commits product scope and capital, the execution rights granted to an automated loop can extend to rewriting interfaces, pipelines, and compiler passes, yet still stop short of commitment. A generator with the authority to rewrite RTL across modules does not thereby gain authority to approve timing waivers, relax signoff constraints, or declare its own output tapeout-ready.

Separating execution from commitment requires a clear record of who decides what. Commitment records specify which design advances, which alternatives were rejected, which conditions the evidence covered, what uncertainty remains, and what triggers would reopen the choice. The division in @tbl-lighthouse-action-rights makes three responsibilities explicit: doing the design work, establishing what its results support, and deciding whether to commit. These responsibilities may involve overlapping teams, but completing one step never authorizes the next.

| **Decision** | **Technical question** | **Boundary** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Execute design work** | What candidate state may this person, model, or tool change, and when must it stop? | Work stays within the declared design space, interfaces, budget, and evaluator boundary. |
| **Establish what a result supports** | What does this check show about this artifact under these conditions and assumptions? | Domain specialists own result validity and domain scope. The architect determines how that result applies to the system decision. |
| **Commit the architecture** | Does the integrated design justify the next consequential transition (e.g., tapeout freeze)? | The named commitment authority decides after considering the architect's system recommendation, alternatives, cross-layer results, specialist concurrences, uncertainty, and residual risk. |
: **Execution, support, and commitment carry different responsibilities.** A successful tool run or a favorable local result cannot silently authorize a system architecture. {#tbl-lighthouse-action-rights tbl-colwidths="[28,34,38]"}

Human-automation research likewise separates selecting a decision from carrying it out [@ParasuramanEtAl2000LevelsAutomation]. In a hardware project, that separation determines who may advance a candidate and on what basis. The named authority records a decision against the architect's recommendation, while the underlying check records remain immutable.

That immutability matters when operating conditions shift or new physical constraints emerge and make earlier results inapplicable. Rather than overwriting old measurements, the team appends fresh checks with their conditions and versions to preserve the basis of the original decision for later diagnosis. An intact record makes that history inspectable, even though it cannot by itself prove that the original checks were sufficient or their assumptions correct. Before a named authority approves a tapeout freeze on the basis of that record, the review must clear three concrete obligations: intellectual-property provenance, containment of residual technical risk, and capital and physical qualification.

### IP Provenance and Indemnification

When an automated generator emits large spans of RTL or millions of netlist lines, structural refactoring, signal renaming, and logic synthesis can disguise memorized third-party or copylefted source logic from simple token scanners. An unguarded prompt can also leak proprietary foundry process design kit (PDK) rules to an external model endpoint. Before committing capital to silicon fabrication, the organization must therefore resolve the IP conditions under which it can use the candidate. For generated RTL, the commitment record should identify the supplied sources, permitted transformations, and checks performed. It should also expose what is unknown about the generator's training data or the origin of an emitted fragment, so that those limits stay visible to the responsible IP reviewers.

How deep those provenance checks must go depends on the scope of generation. Engineers can review a generated leaf module line by line and scan it for token-level similarity. Swept values such as cache depths carry little copyright risk of their own, so legal review shifts to the data used to train performance surrogates. Once an autonomous design system synthesizes multi-tier microarchitectural logic across blocks, however, visual inspection can no longer detect semantic memorization or copyright infringement. The engineering organization then surrounds the design system with four complementary governance controls:

- **Prompt and lineage records**: Retain the supplied specifications, prompts, model checkpoints, random seeds, tool transcripts, and intermediate artifacts with version identities and integrity hashes. A hash such as SHA-256 detects whether an artifact changed, and a digital signature authenticates its signer, but neither establishes where an emitted fragment originated. Restricting retrieval to approved specifications likewise limits the supplied context, and formal equivalence checking can establish correspondence to a reference under declared assumptions, yet neither proves training-data provenance or noninfringement.
- **Similarity and license screening**: Screen generated RTL for recognizable overlap with indexed source repositories and retain the findings for review. A clean scan covers only the sources and similarities the scanner can detect; it is not an origin guarantee.
- **Restricted processing environments**: Declare where foundry PDK rules, cell libraries, third-party commercial IP, and internal protocols may be processed so that restricted materials stay out of training corpora and external model contexts. Restrict tool and network access accordingly, and retain the execution and transfer records needed to check compliance with that boundary.
- **Third-party IP boundaries**: Pin vendor block versions and interface contracts, and limit automated modifications to the scope the organization has authorized. Where internals are unavailable or modification is prohibited, explore integration through the exposed interfaces. Boundary checks can reveal prohibited tool actions without establishing the full legal status of the resulting system.

Together, these controls make the technical history reviewable, though IP acceptance and any indemnification decision still require the organization's separate review rather than following from passing functional checks.

### Managing Residual Risk with Hardware Chicken-Bits

Because some uncertainties remain even when a design approaches freeze, architects often include a hardware chicken-bit that selects an implemented fallback mode through a privileged control register, allowing firmware to disable a risky optimization after fabrication. Simply adding the register, however, does not establish that the fallback contains the fault or preserves the product's requirements. Verification must therefore exercise both its nominal and asserted states along the implemented control path, since a fallback branch left tied to a constant during synthesis may disappear through constant propagation and dead-code elimination.

Consider a constructed Lighthouse example, neither implemented nor measured in the retained study, in which a proposed control staggers activation across NPU multiply-accumulate columns. Simultaneous activation could create a rapid current transient ($di/dt$) and supply-voltage droop that threatens setup timing.[^fn-di-dt-c11] While staggering activation might reduce that transient, it could also lower throughput enough to miss the frame deadline.

To record a trade-off of this kind, a residual-risk statement must connect the failure mode, its consequence, the remaining uncertainty, a detecting check, and any containment action. Here, the mode is voltage droop during burst activation; the consequences include corrupted computation or throttling that misses the frame deadline. Dynamic power-integrity analysis under declared activity and package assumptions would test the droop mechanism, while post-silicon monitors could help detect it if their sensitivity were established. Until those checks run, neither the droop bound nor the proposed control's effectiveness is known. The recommendation must state that gap rather than count the proposed control as protection.

[^fn-di-dt-c11]: **Inductive voltage droop and current transients**: Inductive voltage droop ($V = L \cdot di/dt$) occurs across package and on-chip power distribution inductances when clock gating or simultaneous transistor switching causes rapid changes in current ($di/dt$). The resulting voltage decrease can threaten SRAM state retention or logic timing.

Even when a fallback is verified to contain the fault, the commitment record should still state the performance penalty of relying on it. For latency, a *derating penalty* compares nominal and derated execution under the same workload and operating conditions:[^fn-derating-penalty-c11]

$$
\Delta_{\text{derate}} = \frac{T_{\text{derated}} - T_{\text{nominal}}}{T_{\text{nominal}}}
$$

Here $T_{\text{nominal}}$ and $T_{\text{derated}}$ are the execution times with the ordinary and fallback behavior. For the proposed staggered activation, this penalty remains unmeasured. The fallback must still meet the frame deadline and 3\ W subsystem budget under the conditions in which the team intends to rely on it.

Other fallbacks can change that assessment because if a cache control simultaneously forces write-through operation, its extra memory traffic could alter power and latency while the NPU runs in the derated mode. Verification must therefore cover the legal combinations and their system interactions, not only each control in isolation. Pairwise checks alone do not establish global deadlock freedom, because a cycle of waits may close only when three or more controls are active together; hierarchical proofs help when their composition assumptions hold. Beyond interaction effects, the control path itself must remain usable under the fault it is meant to contain; when a fault lies in physical circuitry, a restriction on how the part is used may limit exposure without repairing the fault, as Intel's Cougar Point chipset showed [@Intel2011CougarPoint; @Intel2011CougarPointUpdate].

[^fn-derating-penalty-c11]: **Microarchitectural derating penalty**: This book's derating penalty, distinct from the on-chip-variation derates that static timing analysis applies to path delays, measures the slowdown from nominal performance when post-silicon workarounds (such as serialization or wait states) must be engaged to avoid physical timing violations, dynamic voltage droop, or race conditions under worst-case thermal and voltage corners.

::: {.callout-war-story title="A correction must reach the physical failure"}
**The claim.** On January 31, 2011, Intel disclosed a design issue in its 6 Series chipset, code-named Cougar Point, which shipped in systems built on Sandy Bridge processors. Intel stated that consumers could continue to use their systems with confidence while manufacturers arranged a permanent solution [@Intel2011CougarPoint].

**The gap.** The defect was physical. Serial ATA (SATA) ports in the chipset could degrade over time, affecting attached drives. Intel's correction was a revised chipset. It stopped shipping the affected part, began manufacturing a corrected version, and estimated about \$700 million to repair and replace affected materials and systems, alongside a roughly \$300 million first-quarter revenue reduction. A week later, at the request of computer makers, Intel resumed shipping the original part for use only in system configurations the issue did not affect [@Intel2011CougarPointUpdate].

**The lesson.** A containment mechanism helps only if it reaches or avoids the mechanism that fails. A proposed workaround must be checked against the physical failure class it claims to contain. Restricting a part to unaffected configurations can contain new exposure by avoiding the fault, but it corrects nothing in the silicon.
:::

Even a passing derated check would establish only that the declared fallback stays within the requirements and conditions actually tested, not that the product is commercially viable or insulated from financial risk.

Shipping an uncharacterized feature disabled by default creates a related obligation. Its disabled state must preserve baseline requirements, its enable path must stay restricted to authorized modes, and reset and fault handling must maintain that separation. The exception needs an owner and a review trigger tied to characterization. Otherwise, temporary exceptions can become accepted practice without the evidence originally required [@Vaughan1996Challenger].

To keep temporary search relaxations from hardening into release policy, automated exploration may investigate relaxed constraints in an isolated workspace, but the responsible specialists must approve any change to release constraints or waivers. Their record preserves the technical justification, affected conditions, checks, and reconsideration trigger, though a signature identifies the approver without proving the exception sound. When a risk remains unacceptable and no verified avoidance or containment exists, the candidate cannot advance, and any decision to accept a bounded risk without containment requires an explicit rationale from the responsible authority.

### Capital Allocation and Physical Qualification

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Errata study: every number in this section is read from the committed data in
# data/studies/01-silicon-errata-archaeology/ (errata_classified.csv, sources.csv,
# audit_metrics.json, merge_rule_sensitivity.json, withdrawn_rows.csv,
# excluded_rows.csv). Reproduce with the commands in that folder's README.
import csv
import json
from pathlib import Path

import _python.plots as _ap

_errata_dir = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "data/studies/01-silicon-errata-archaeology"
# Rows with no retained or retrievable primary text stay in the CSV as evidence and
# leave every count, the same way audit_metrics.load_population() drops them.
_excluded = list(csv.DictReader(
    line for line in (_errata_dir / "excluded_rows.csv").open(encoding="utf-8") if not line.startswith("#")
))
_drop = {(r["family"], r["erratum_id"]) for r in _excluded}
_errata = [
    r for r in csv.DictReader((_errata_dir / "errata_classified.csv").open(encoding="utf-8"))
    if (r["family"], r["erratum_id"]) not in _drop
]
_sources = list(csv.DictReader(
    line for line in (_errata_dir / "sources.csv").open(encoding="utf-8") if not line.startswith("#")
))
_audit = json.loads((_errata_dir / "audit_metrics.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
_words = "zero one two three four five six seven eight nine ten eleven twelve".split()


def _pct(x):
    return f"{100 * x:.0f}"


def _ci(pair):
    return f"{100 * pair[0]:.0f} to {100 * pair[1]:.0f}"


errata_n = f"{len(_errata):,}"
families_n = len(_sources)
intel_families = sum(r["vendor"] == "Intel" for r in _sources)
amd_families = families_n - intel_families
audited_n = _audit["audited"]
agree_pct = _pct(_audit["agreement_weighted"])
agree_ci = _ci(_audit["agreement_weighted_ci95"])
_sh = _audit["shares"]
_mem = _sh["Memory controller, coherence fabric, and I/O"]
mem_adj, mem_ci = _pct(_mem["adjusted_share"]), _ci(_mem["adjusted_ci95"])
arith_n = _words[_audit["arithmetic_datapath_audited"]]
no_fix_pct = _pct(_audit["status_counts"]["No Fix"] / len(_errata))

# Composition of the class that joins I/O with memory controllers and coherence, by rule label.
_by_rule = {}
for _r in _errata:
    _by_rule[_r["subsystem"]] = _by_rule.get(_r["subsystem"], 0) + 1
_io = _by_rule["I/O and peripheral interfaces"]
_mc = _by_rule["Memory controller and DRAM"]
_coh = _by_rule["Coherence and on-die or socket fabric"]
io_of_class_pct = _pct(_io / (_io + _mc + _coh))
memsys_rule_pct = f"{100 * (_mc + _coh + _by_rule['Caches, TLBs, and load-store ordering']) / len(_errata):.1f}"

# Class-order spans describe the classifier over title matches only; other rows stay as assigned.
# No largest share or ranking is reported.
_merge = json.loads((_errata_dir / "merge_rule_sensitivity.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
failed_word = _words[len(_merge["failed_classes"])].capitalize()
_mct = _merge["machine_check_target"]
_to_ix = "Instruction execution and exceptions"
_to_irq = "Interrupts, timers, reset, and system management"
mc_ix_word = _words[_mct["rows"][_to_ix]]
mc_irq_word = _words[_mct["rows"][_to_irq]]
mc_same_title_word = _words[_mct["rows"][_to_ix] - _mct["distinct_titles"][_to_ix] + 1]
_memsys = _merge["memory_system_any_grouping"]
memsys_adj_pct, memsys_adj_ci = f"{100 * _memsys['adjusted_share']:.0f}", _ci(_memsys["adjusted_ci95"])
_single = _merge["single_label_changes"]["memory_system_adjusted_range"]
memsys_one_low, memsys_one_high = _pct(_single[0]), _pct(_single[1])
memsys_agree, memsys_audited = _memsys["agree"], _memsys["audited"]
memsys_precision, memsys_wilson = _pct(_memsys["precision_sample"]), _pct(_memsys["wilson_low"])
memsys_title_pct = f"{100 * _memsys['distinct_title_share']:.1f}"
_order = _merge["class_order"]
order_n = f"{_order['orders']:,}"
order_multi, order_title = f"{_order['title_matched_more_than_one_class']:,}", f"{_order['title_matched']:,}"
order_held = len(_errata) - _order["title_matched"]
order_mem_low, order_mem_high = _pct(_order["memory_system_rule_share_range"][0]), _pct(_order["memory_system_rule_share_range"][1])
_top = _order["largest_merged_class"]
order_drawn_low, order_drawn_high = (_pct(x) for x in _top["as_applied"]["share_range"])
order_written_low, order_written_high = (_pct(x) for x in _top["written_rule"]["share_range"])

# Rows whose pinned source is gone: the vendor removed them and no copy is held.
_withdrawn = list(csv.DictReader(
    line for line in (_errata_dir / "withdrawn_rows.csv").open(encoding="utf-8") if not line.startswith("#")
))
withdrawn_word = _words[len(_withdrawn)]
withdrawn_fam_word = _words[len({r["family"] for r in _withdrawn})]
assert {(r["family"], r["erratum_id"]) for r in _withdrawn} == _drop, "every withdrawn row is excluded"
assert len(_errata) == _audit["population"], "chapter and study use the same rows"

_s18_sum = json.loads((_errata_dir.parent / "18-errata-by-year" / "summary.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
launch_yr_min, launch_yr_max = _s18_sum["launch_year_range"]

```

Advancing from simulation to silicon commits NRE capital for mask tooling and physical qualification.[^fn-mask-nre-c11] Faster candidate generation does not reduce the mask charge for a chosen process or remove the cost of containing defects after fabrication. Published processor errata list defects found in shipped parts, which shows what that obligation covers. Our retained analysis covers `{python} errata_n` itemized errata across `{python} families_n` CPU families (`{python} intel_families` from Intel and `{python} amd_families` from AMD) introduced between `{python} launch_yr_min` and `{python} launch_yr_max` [@Intel2022XeonE5v4SpecUpdate; @Intel2020XeonScalableSpecUpdate; @Intel2023XeonScalableGen2SpecUpdate; @Intel2026XeonScalableGen3SpecUpdate; @Intel2026XeonScalableGen4SpecUpdate; @Intel2026XeonScalableGen5SpecUpdate; @Intel2025Core8th9thGenSpecUpdate; @Intel2026Core10thGenSpecUpdate; @Intel2026Core11thGenTigerLakeSpecUpdate; @Intel2023Core11thGenRocketLakeSpecUpdate; @Intel2026Core12thGenSpecUpdate; @Intel2026Core13th14thGenSpecUpdate; @Intel2026CoreUltraSpecUpdate; @Intel2026CoreUltra200VSpecUpdate; @Intel2026CoreUltraSeries2SpecUpdate; @AMD2023Family17h00hRevisionGuide; @AMD2026Family17h30hRevisionGuide; @AMD2025Family19h10hRevisionGuide; @AMD2025Family1Ah00hRevisionGuide]. The extracted identifiers match the summary table in each document we can still fetch at its pinned revision. Intel has since revised the other five, and we neither retain those pinned revisions nor can fetch them, so the only evidence of their match is the columns the study recorded. Most of their rows survive in the later revisions, but `{python} withdrawn_word` rows from `{python} withdrawn_fam_word` families have no reachable source. The October 2026 revisions mark those entries as removed, and because we hold no copy of their earlier text, nobody can check the titles and statuses the study recorded for them. We therefore leave them out of the `{python} errata_n` errata counted here and keep them in the study files only as a record of what was excluded.

[^fn-mask-nre-c11]: **Mask tooling non-recurring engineering and physical signoff**: A reticle mask set is an upfront capital expenditure, with at least one photomask for each patterned layer, paid before any production wafer is processed. One analyst estimate from 2022 puts a mask set above \$1 million at 28\ nm, above \$10 million at 7\ nm, and pushing into the \$40 million range as processes cross 3\ nm [@Patel2022MaskSetCosts]. A revision needs at least some new masks and a few months of fabrication [@Patel2022MaskSetCosts], so a respin repeats part of this charge.

When we ask where those retained errata fall across a processor, memory controllers, coherence fabrics, and caches admit many interleavings of concurrent requests, so their large verification state spaces might lead us to expect a concentration of published defects there. Arithmetic units, with comparatively compact specifications and mature formal checks, might appear less exposed. Subsystem counts let us examine that expectation descriptively, though they do not measure verification difficulty or defect probability.

The classifier that produces those subsystem counts is rule-based and model-assisted, with no human label audit. Retained keyword rules assign each erratum to a class, and one model relabeled a stratified sample of `{python} audited_n` errata (@fig-errata-subsystem-shares). The rule labels agree with that reading on an estimated `{python} agree_pct`% of the corpus (95% interval `{python} agree_ci`%). The study has no independent human labels, so the adjusted shares are estimates from one model's reading of that sample rather than independently verified ground truth. They also rest on extracted entry text that has had no field-level check, and the same extractor produced workaround fields we withdrew after confirming parsing errors.[^fn-errata-audit-c11]

[^fn-errata-audit-c11]: **Errata classification test**: The study reports a class alone only if at least 70% of its sampled rule labels hold under the model's relabeling and the lower Wilson bound reaches 50%. Its written rule merges a failed class with the class the model most often relabeled it as when the merged class passes the same test, and drops the class otherwise. The rule does not say what to do when two classes tie. Earlier versions of the study's class file recorded the rule as fixed before any merge, but the rule and the merges first appear in the same commit, so the record cannot show the order. The study records that one model wrote the rules and labeled the sample, which the retained files cannot show. The script that builds the relabeling worksheet omits the rule labels, but the worksheet was not retained, so we cannot show what the labeler saw, and hiding those labels would not remove shared assumptions in any case. No person has relabeled the stratified sample. The retained study includes the rules, sample, class consolidations, and the shares under every reading discussed here.

![**The ranking of published CPU errata classes depends on how a rule-based classifier orders its classes.** Shares of `{python} errata_n` errata from the specification updates and revision guides of `{python} families_n` Intel and AMD CPU families, in the six classes the study applied and one recorded class order. Bars give the share keyword rules assign. Dots and whiskers give the share adjusted by one model's relabeling of a stratified sample of `{python} audited_n` errata, with no human label audit and with 95% intervals that hold grouping and order fixed. The order of the bars is not a finding. The hatched bar holds errata that no rule matched and two dropped classes.](images/fig-errata-subsystem-shares){#fig-errata-subsystem-shares width="100%" fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart of published CPU errata shares for six subsystem classes and a hatched bar for errata not resolved to a class, drawn for one grouping and one class order. The bars are sorted by length from I/O with memory controllers and coherence, through debug and performance monitoring, core execution with caches and translation lookaside buffers, and virtualization and security, down to power and interrupts. Each bar carries a dot with an interval marking an estimate adjusted by a model, and several dots sit past the ends of their bars."}

@fig-errata-subsystem-shares draws the grouping the study applied, which departs from its written merge rule. `{python} failed_word` classes failed the relabeling test. Caches and security features merged as the rule directs. Coherence joined I/O and memory controllers, although the model most often relabeled its entries as power errata, a merge that passes, and although memory controllers had passed alone. Graphics and machine-check errata were dropped into the hatched bar, which is as long by rule as any reported class, although merges with I/O and with instruction execution both pass.

The written rule would not settle the ranking either, because its most consequential step rests on a small count. The model relabeled `{python} mc_ix_word` machine-check rows as instruction execution and `{python} mc_irq_word` as interrupts, and `{python} mc_same_title_word` of the first group are one erratum title published for two families. If we count each title once, as the distinct-title shares do, the two targets tie, and the rule does not say which to take. The 95% intervals hold the grouping and the labels fixed, so they do not cover this choice.

The ranking also depends on how a rule-based classifier orders its classes. The rules try the classes in a fixed order and keep the first match, and `{python} order_multi` of the `{python} order_title` entries matched on their titles match more than one class. Our test of that dependence reorders only those title matches. It shuffles the class order at random for them and holds the other `{python} order_held` entries as first assigned, even though the entries matched on description text also depend on class order. Across `{python} order_n` such title-only orders, the largest class by rule runs from about `{python} order_drawn_low`% to about `{python} order_drawn_high`% of the corpus in the grouping as drawn, and the class that comes out largest changes with the order. Under the written merge rule it runs from about `{python} order_written_low`% to about `{python} order_written_high`%. Because the description matches never move, neither span bounds the complete classifier, and both describe the classifier rather than the processors. Only the recorded order has a relabeled sample, so we report neither a largest share nor a ranking as a finding about silicon errata.

A narrower result bears on the expectation that prompted the count. Memory controllers, coherence fabrics, and caches together account for `{python} memsys_rule_pct`% of the corpus by rule and an estimated `{python} memsys_adj_pct`% after the model's relabeling (95% interval `{python} memsys_adj_ci`%), and neither figure depends on how the classes are merged. We chose this sum after seeing the rule counts, and we lean on it here because broader statements about the largest class failed audit, so it is a description rather than a planned test. As a class it fails the study's reporting test, with `{python} memsys_agree` of `{python} memsys_audited` sampled rule labels holding (`{python} memsys_precision`%, lower Wilson bound `{python} memsys_wilson`%). The adjusted estimate therefore carries the result, and the rule figure is context. Any one-label change to the relabeled sample keeps that estimate between `{python} memsys_one_low`% and `{python} memsys_one_high`%. The rule figure does depend on class order, and across the same title-only orders it runs from `{python} order_mem_low`% to `{python} order_mem_high`%. The sum stays at about a quarter of the corpus or less in every reading we tested, although the adjusted estimate exists only for the recorded order. In the grouping and class order as drawn, one class combines I/O and peripheral interfaces with memory controllers and coherence fabrics. Its estimated share after the model's relabeling is `{python} mem_adj`% (95% interval `{python} mem_ci`%), and `{python} io_of_class_pct`% of its rule-assigned entries concern I/O and peripherals. Core execution, caches, and translation lookaside buffers (TLBs) form a second class, and the debug and monitoring logic that observes execution forms a third. Arithmetic datapath defects are uncommon in the relabeled sample: `{python} arith_n` of `{python} audited_n` entries describe a floating-point, integer, or vector unit that computes or schedules incorrectly. Many documented behaviors instead concern control and integration. A virtual-machine entry that clears the trace-enable bit can emit a spurious trace packet [@Intel2020XeonScalableSpecUpdate], and after a C6 sleep-state exit the processor can dispatch a queued interrupt before an earlier one of the same priority completes [@Intel2022XeonE5v4SpecUpdate].

Both those control examples and the broader subsystem shares describe customer-facing documents rather than a complete census of defects, since each class records the behavior a document reports rather than the circuit where the defect originates. They lack denominators for subsystem size or complexity, use classes of unequal scope, and draw mostly on Intel documents. Erratum titles also recur across processor families, though matching wording does not establish identical hardware root causes. In the recorded class order, counting distinct titles changes the shares and puts the memory-system sum at `{python} memsys_title_pct`% of titles. While the counts therefore cannot establish escape rates or test the state-space explanation, they do show why ownership must extend across power-state transitions, interrupts, isolation, interfaces, and diagnostic logic, rather than end at a correctly computed arithmetic result.

The documents also record whether a fix is planned or has been made, and `{python} no_fix_pct`% of the corpus carries no planned fix. When dispositions differ across steppings, the extraction keeps the least resolved one, so this share is an upper reading of entries with no fix on any stepping. It describes entries across the covered variants, not the fraction of shipped processors with an active defect or the availability of a workaround. Any workaround relied on in a commitment still needs functional checks and measured costs under its intended conditions.

Rather than comparing generated RTL with human-written RTL, these findings identify behaviors an AI-native design system must address if it generates control and integration logic, along with the responsibilities its architect must carry into commitment review. The complete workflow comparison must therefore count the effort of checking those control and integration behaviors (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect), whereas the product decision separately weighs physical readiness, remaining expenditure, shipment volume, and residual risk (@sec-design-cost-pressure).

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The Lighthouse commitment remains open"}
**Context.** Freezing a Level-2 cache capacity or selecting an accelerator organization for the Lighthouse mobile XR subsystem would constrain later software, memory, and physical implementation choices.

**Application.** Before such a freeze, the architect must establish that the selected organization meets its workload requirements within the subsystem's memory, power, and physical constraints. The required physical signoff, power modeling, and system-level checks remain missing.

**Outcome.** The supported recommendation is to obtain the missing system evidence before advancing toward freeze or tapeout. The person responsible for the product would still need to assess the resulting recommendation across all eight requirement domains (@sec-intent-vs-spec) and record a decision.
:::

Gathering that system evidence requires a verification plan that connects each required property to qualified specialist evidence (@sec-mapping-requirements-toolchains), including implementation correspondence, physical timing, power and package behavior, and manufacturing test readiness where the transition requires them. Missing required evidence prevents advancement.

## Sustaining Architectural Ownership {#sec-sustaining-responsibility}

Architectural ownership continues as teams integrate revisions and as deployed silicon encounters new conditions. It requires access to the specifications, models, traces, signoff reports, and rejected alternatives needed to investigate a recommendation, together with authority to stop or reopen it. Naming a reviewer without that access or authority separates responsibility from control. Research on automation bias likewise warns against substituting an automated recommendation for independent examination [@SkitkaEtAl1999AutomationBias].

::: {.callout-law title="Moral Crumple Zones and Nondelegable Signoff"}
**The Classical Principle:** A human operator becomes a *moral crumple zone* when they absorb responsibility for failures of an automated system they could not meaningfully inspect or halt [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones]. The term describes an organizational mismatch between responsibility and operational control, not a rule assigning legal liability.

**The Hardware Trap:** A signing engineer may bear the blame for a generated block without having had the access, time, or authority to review it meaningfully.

**The Architectural Antidote:** Pair every signoff with review access, decision authority, and an inspectable commitment record, and declare residual risk explicitly before commitment (@sec-law-moral-crumple-zones in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

### Keeping Recommendations Valid During Integration {#sec-sustaining-alignment-churn}

An architectural recommendation can become stale before silicon reaches the foundry because engineers and automated loops continue changing RTL, device drivers, compiler backends, and firmware while the project is under evaluation. To keep the recommendation anchored as those artifacts move, the architect ties each recommendation to an integration snapshot, states which changes require fresh checks, and sets explicit boundaries for external protocols, clock crossings, and register maps whenever subblock optimization is delegated.

As subsequent edits land against that snapshot, continuous integration runs equivalence, timing, and interface checks at a fidelity matched to the changed artifacts, while full physical qualification covers the integrated candidate proposed for commitment. A local change that preserves its source-level interface can still alter cross-block timing or power, so a clean merge does not establish that the earlier recommendation remains valid.

Variation on a fixed snapshot needs a different diagnosis. If a tuning pass succeeds on one seed and fails timing on another, the team must distinguish different generated candidates from different implementation outcomes for the same candidate. The former concerns search behavior; the latter may expose marginal closure or tool sensitivity. The recommendation states which variation was tested and which conditions it covers, using the execution and comparison discipline already developed in @sec-incremental-churn-dispersion and @sec-evidence-specific-to-claim-and-scope.
